newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin out to show he in charge in keynote speech.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin out to show he in charge in keynote speech.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin was set on Thursday to launch a crusade against corruption and try to show he is firmly in charge in Russia in a state of the nation address to parliament.
A government shake-up was widely expected to be announced later in the day, either by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin or by Yeltsin.

Kremlin sources said Yeltsin's chief of staff, the liberal Anatoly Chubais, could be taken on as Chernomyrdin's first deputy premier to spearhead the crackdown on economic crime, which is choking Russia's reforms.

"Russia entered 1997 with a heavy load of problems...More than half its citizens are suffering from delays in wage and pension payments," Yeltsin declared in a written address on which the speech, starting at 0800 GMT, is based.
"The stranglehold of non-payment is paralysing the economy and the state apparatus is being corroded by corruption," he said. "The authorities barely manage to put laws and decrees into effect."
Yeltsin's speech was expected to last half an hour, official sources said.

It will be a big test of the 66-year-old leader's health after he spent the first eight months of his second term out of action, first because of heart problems and bypass surgery in November and then because of pneumonia.
Yeltsin chided Chernomyrdin last week for the government's poor performance and urged him to put things right immediately.
The liberal Izvestia newspaper said on Thursday that it expected Chubais to be appointed number two in the government and take charge of running everyday affairs.

It said Finance Minister Alexander Livshits, first deputy prime ministers Vladimir Potanin and Viktor Ilyushin, Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Lobov and Labour and Social Development Minister Gennady Melikyan were likely to be dismissed.

In his written address, the president made clear that first and foremost he wanted the prime minister to restore order. Otherwise organised crime and corruption threatened to choke the life out of his post-Soviet democratic market reforms.
"An effective market economy is not just freedom for private enterprise but also a strict legal order -- common, stable and generally observed rules of economic activity," Yeltsin said.
"The task of the state is to set such rules and to make sure they are obeyed."

"The problem of economic crime and corruption has grown from what was clearly a police matter into a political issue. The criminal world has in fact openly challenged the state and launched into an open competition with it," he said.
"When free buying and selling extends to the passing of laws, to the work of civil servants and to court decisions, it is not just immoral but a mortal danger to society and the state."
The text, in contrast to last year's, was short on concrete economic proposals. Some analysts suggest Yeltsin wants to give Chubais, 41, a free hand to deal with the economy.

Chubais, an outstanding administrator, is popular with foreign investors but hated by the communists who dominate parliament and who accuse him of corruption in his management of Russia's privatisation drive.
Chernomyrdin was due to chair a government meeting on Thursday afternoon at which he could announce his reshuffle. Izvestia said Yeltsin may choose to announce it himself.
